title: Superstate exposes two redemption routes distinguished only by which rate-limit key they consume
content:
The Superstate USTB instance is the first in this run to populate its `Rate Limit IDs` slot with actual values (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.6.1.2.3): `USTB_DEPOSIT` and `USTB_REDEEM` both against `0x43415eB6ff9DB7E26A15b704e7A3eDCe97d31C4e` — the instance's own Token Address — and a third entry, "`USTB_REDEEM` (instant liquidity)", against a different address `0x4c21B7577C8FE8b0B0669165ee7C8f67fa1454Cf`.

Two things are notable. The values recorded are contract addresses, not the 32-byte derived keys published for the wETH and Maple USDT instances — consistent with `makeAssetKey(LIMIT_NAME, asset)` taking an address as its second argument, but it means the slot is populated with an input to the key rather than the key itself, and the same value serves two opposite directions.

More substantively, redemption is split. A standard `USTB_REDEEM` and an instant-liquidity `USTB_REDEEM` are separate rate-limit entries, so Spark can size its fast exit independently of its slow one. That is the correct shape for a tokenised-treasury venue where instant redemption draws on a limited liquidity buffer while standard redemption settles against the underlying portfolio.

It is also the first place in these instances where the Artifact acknowledges at the parameter level that exit speed and exit size trade against each other. Elsewhere the outflow leg is a single `Unlimited`; here the two exit routes are distinct budgets, which is the only way to express 'we may leave quickly, but only this much quickly'.
description: USTB lists USTB_DEPOSIT and USTB_REDEEM against the token address plus a second USTB_REDEEM for instant liquidity at a different address — the fast and slow exits are separated at the limit layer.
